01 COURT IS NOW IN SESSION

Yesterday, old friends.
Today, complete strangers.

You're sick of studying kanji. Fair enough. You sit down, open your materials and concentrate. Look at the character. Read the meaning. Nod with the quiet authority of someone who has finally cracked it.

Next day, same character. Absolute void. It could mean “gratitude”, “refrigerator” or be the logo of a printer with a personal grudge.

So you deliver your verdict: “I have a terrible memory.” Quite a ruling. You've put an entire organ on trial, without a lawyer, for failing to absorb a writing system you may have met on Tuesday.

DoDon is appealing the verdict. He enjoys a courtroom entrance. And your brain deserves a better defence than “but I read it”.

02 A SMALL COMPATIBILITY ISSUE

Japanese wasn't
pre-installed.

If you grew up reading an alphabet, you've had years of practice recognising certain shapes and putting them together. Much of it now feels obvious. Then kanji arrive, and the Department of Obvious closes for stocktaking.

You have to learn which details matter, which components recur, and how shapes connect to meanings and readings. Where an experienced reader sees familiar structures, you may initially see a tangle. Familiarity takes practice: speaking a language from birth and reading its script are different skills.

In experiments with Chinese characters, experienced readers showed visual-memory advantages linked to their knowledge of written forms; beginners also improved for characters they had practised. The study concerns Chinese, but illustrates a useful point here too: experience with those shapes matters. Mercifully, a passport is not a cognitive function. [1]

忘

JAPAN HAS A SENSE OF HUMOUR

There's a kanji
for “forget”.

This one. In 忘れる, wasureru, it means “to forget”. Yes: to discuss the kanji you forget, you can learn another kanji.

A level of audacity we respect. [5]

What about evolution? It didn't hand you a universal reader with kanji already configured. Under the neuronal recycling hypothesis, learning to read repurposes existing brain circuits for a relatively recent cultural skill. Your brain can adapt. It's learning a trade, not opening an attachment. [2]

The useful question becomes: how do we teach it that trade without turning every evening into an industrial dispute?

MEANWHILE, AT HEAD OFFICE

“One symbol, one sound.”
What a lovely thought.

Take 生. In 学生 (gakusei, “student”), its reading is sei. In 生きる (ikiru, “to live”), the kanji is read i. On its own, 生 (nama) can mean raw or uncooked. [6]

Same character; the word tells you what job it's doing. Learning it in real words gives you something to hold on to. Tackling every reading in one evening is a meeting invitation you really should have declined.

One kanji. Three examples. Your patience on the table.
WordReadingMeaningDoDon's note
学生gakuseistudentYou, at present.
生きるikiruto livePlease continue while studying.
生namaraw, uncookedLike your knowledge before a little review.

And no, kanji aren't all tiny pictures waiting to be guessed. 森 (“forest”) offers you three 木 (“tree”): thank you, very cooperative. A concept like “intention” is rather harder to photograph. Components, words and examples help build connections. An invented story can be a useful mnemonic; explaining a character's origin calls for a dictionary. Even prophets need a bibliography. [7]

03 THE MIRACLE OF “BUT I KNEW THAT”

The answer underneath
is a superb prompter.

You look at a card again and it all seems familiar. Lovely. But with the meaning still sitting there, you haven't checked whether you can retrieve it yourself. You've checked that you can read the answer. A respectable talent; questionable exam conditions.

Let's try something tiny. One kanji, one meaning. Then we dismiss the prompter. DoDon is already wearing his “I knew all along” expression.

“Let's try that without the autocue.”

A LITTLE SOFA-BASED EXPERIMENT

忘

to forget

Look at the shape and connect it to the meaning. We've met it already, so you even have the benefit of an encore.

忘

忘 → to forget

A game to notice the difference between seeing an answer and looking for it in memory. It neither grades your brain nor measures long-term retention.

Whether you got it or not, you've changed the task: you tried to recall an answer. Retrieval practice can help later remembering. In a classic study, practising recall of studied material led to better retention after several days than rereading alone, even though rereading made students feel more confident. Recognise that slightly theatrical confidence? [3]

When an answer won't come, check it, work out what was missing and return to it. An error shows you where to work. DoDon may be a show-off, but he doesn't demand an identity crisis with every wrong answer.

FIRST COMMANDMENT, UNANIMOUSLY APPROVED BY DODON

“Kanji won't get in
by osmosis.
We've checked.”

Osmosis has other commitments. Try remembering without looking.

MEMORY HAS A SEQUEL. OUR APOLOGIES.

Review.
A sequel worth making.

You remembered once. Excellent. Now resist declaring the character a permanent World Heritage Site in your head.

Spacing study across time can support long-term memory better than cramming every repetition into one sitting. Useful review intervals also depend on how long you want to retain something. No single blessed schedule fits every person and every item. [4]

A spaced repetition system, or SRS, organises these returns and helps decide what to review. You supply the attempt, check the answer and pay some attention. The system handles the diary. The sort of division of labour one expects from a functioning civilisation.

04 AND LO, A FISH APPEARED

CONSISTENCY IS A VIRTUE. WE GAVE IT CARD PACKS.

For us mere mortals,
Kanjidon.

You've got the method. That leaves one small masterpiece of human organisation: wanting to do it again tomorrow.

We could have prescribed “more discipline” and retired, pleased with ourselves. Instead, we founded a modest little card cult. DoDon already had the cape. It would have been wasteful.

Kanjidon is our exceedingly humble answer: an app for learning Japanese kanji with collectible cards, quizzes and spaced repetition. We took the liberty of making the next session inviting. Duty had been running the place for years and, frankly, its parties were dreadful.

The cards make an entrance. The quizzes ask the questions. SRS keeps the diary. Open packs, discover kanji and grow your collection. Quizzes put what you're learning to the test; reviews bring you back to it over time. Curiosity gets you through the door, then there's some actual remembering to do. Even our prophet knows how to delegate.

“Let's see which card I get” can be an excellent excuse to start. And when an answer finally comes to you, the credit is yours. DoDon will still accept flowers.

The game brings you back. Review helps the kanji stay. That's the idea. Humility is pencilled in for a later update.

05 A RITUAL FOR PEOPLE WITH LIVES

You can start
without joining a monastery.

Four moves to fit the time you have. The International Conference on the Perfect Study Method can carry on without you. Three hours in, they're still choosing a font.

  1. 01

    Review what you've already met.

    Start with a small batch of reviews. Your older cards have noticed you eyeing the new ones and would appreciate a word.

  2. 02

    Try before you peek.

    Look for the answer, then check it. If it won't come, revisit it. The personal drama is optional and takes ages.

  3. 03

    Give the kanji a word to live in.

    Connect shape, reading and meaning to an example you understand. A lone symbol struggles at parties.

  4. 04

    Leave room for the next round.

    Add cards at a sustainable pace and return to your reviews. If you want to write them by hand, practise that too: admiring them doesn't move the pen.

DROP-IN AUDIENCES

The prophet will see you now.

How do I persuade a kanji to stay until tomorrow?

Give it chances to become familiar: study its shape, connect it to a word, try recalling the meaning without looking, then check. Return to it at different times. Remembering kanji means cultivating these encounters. A quick read is a polite nod in the lift; a dinner invitation requires a little more familiarity.

Pen and paper: how do I review with a little style?

Look at the components, cover the model, try writing it and compare. You practise reconstructing the shape and find the details you're missing. Make time for handwriting if that's a skill you want. Spotting a stroke you used to overlook is a small connoisseur's pleasure. DoDon approves. His own signature takes up half a page.

One kanji, several readings: who gets invited first?

The readings in the words you're studying. Meeting 学生? Start with gakusei and “student”. Expand the circle as new words arrive. The dictionary keeps the full guest list; you can host one dinner at a time. Even DoDon respects the practicalities of seating.

What does a session with His Packness look like?

Open Kanjidon and start with your reviews: answers to retrieve, details to bring back into focus. Then explore cards and content at a pace you can sustain. Packs and collecting supply the curiosity; quizzes and spaced repetition organise the memory work. You bring the attention. Stage presence is very much covered.

I'm aiming for the JLPT. Does the prophet travel?

He's packed his good cape. Kanjidon includes content from N5 to N1, pairing kanji with vocabulary, grammar, reading and listening. Choose your level, work on areas that need attention and build your preparation piece by piece. Explore the app's learning path here. DoDon appreciates advance notice. He needs to rehearse the pep talk.

The cape was our idea. These studies support the points on visual experience, reading, retrieval and distributed practice; they are not studies of Kanjidon's effectiveness.

  1. Zimmer & Fischer, 2020 · Character expertise and visual memory

    Experiments with experienced readers and beginners: advantages linked to knowledge of written forms. Chinese characters, not a direct test of kanji study with an app.

  2. Dehaene & Cohen, 2007 · Neuronal recycling

    The neuronal recycling hypothesis for cultural skills such as reading.

  3. Roediger & Karpicke, 2006 · Retrieval practice

    Retrieval practice and recall after several days. The experiments used prose passages, not kanji.

  4. Cepeda et al., 2006 · Distributed practice

    A quantitative review of distributed study and the role of spacing intervals.

  5. Kanjipedia · 忘れる

    Meaning and reading of the verb “to forget”.
